issues.legal_issue: A statutory abolition of an impartible hereditary service estate followed by regrant to its former holder does not make ancestral estate the holder’s separate property, and the regranted property is partible among the joint family members.
material_facts: The lands were attached to a hereditary office and had been impartible under the rule of primogeniture.
The senior male family member succeeded to the watan under the pre-existing law and received a regrant after abolition of the watan.
The other family members claimed partition of the lands; there was no finding that they had renounced their rights of succession.
issues.conclusion: The regrant enured to the benefit of the joint Hindu family, and the lands became partible joint family property. The claimant was entitled to a share, and the decree granting partition was restored.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 3 and 5 of the Maharashtra Revenue Patels (Abolition of Office) Act, 1962 extinguish the watan and its incidents, including the service obligation and the rule of primogeniture; the land is regranted to the watandar as an occupant. The regrant does not convert ancestral watan land into the watandar’s separate property. An impartible ancestral estate may remain joint family property, and the senior member’s right to take by survivorship persists unless the junior members expressly or impliedly renounce succession. The Court relied on Nagesh Bisto Desai v. Khando Tirmal Desai, Dattatraya v. Krishna Rao and Anant Kibe v. Purushottam Rao; it also noted that Kalgonda Babgonda was reversed and that Shiddappa Satappa Murugude was decided without notice of the controlling three-Judge decisions.

rule.if: partition_claim_concerning_hereditary_service_land and ancestral_joint_family_estate and estate_was_impartible_under_primogeniture and land_was_regranted_after_abolition

predicates.partition_claim_concerning_hereditary_se: A claimant brought a proceeding seeking partition of land attached to a hereditary service estate.
predicates.ancestral_joint_family_estate: The land was ancestral property of a joint family.
predicates.estate_was_impartible_under_primogenitur: The estate was impartible under a rule giving succession preference to the senior family member.
predicates.land_was_regranted_after_abolition: After the hereditary office and its incidents were abolished, the land was regranted to the former holder.

issues.definition: When an ancestral joint family estate was impartible under primogeniture and is regranted after abolition of its hereditary service character, the regranted land remains joint family property and is partible.

issues.legal_issue: A coparcener’s possession of joint family property does not become adverse to another coparcener without clear and unequivocal proof of an exclusive hostile claim, known to the other member, maintained for the required period.
material_facts: The claimant sought partition after regrant made the lands partible.
The opposing family member relied on mutation and possession as showing exclusive ownership.

Possession could be referred to the family’s lawful joint title, and there was no pleading and proof that the opposing member asserted exclusive hostile title to the claimant’s knowledge or that the claimant acquiesced in it for the statutory period.
issues.conclusion: The opposing member did not acquire title by adverse possession.
issues.legal_principle: Article 65 of the Schedule to the Limitation Act, 1963 places the burden on the person claiming adverse possession to prove clear and unequivocal hostile possession amounting to a denial of the true owner’s title. Possession referable to lawful title is not adverse. In a Hindu joint family, possession by one member is ordinarily treated as possession on behalf of all; mutation for collection of rent or revenue does not by itself prove a hostile act. The claimant must prove an exclusive hostile assertion to the other member’s knowledge, exclusion from enjoyment, and continuation for the statutory period.

predicates.adverse_title_claim_against_coparcener: A person in a family-property dispute claimed ownership by adverse possession against another coparcener.
predicates.possession_traceable_to_joint_title: The possessor’s occupation could be explained by the family’s lawful joint title or possession on behalf of the family.
predicates.no_known_exclusive_hostile_assertion_pro: The claimant did not prove that the possessor clearly asserted exclusive hostile ownership to the claimant’s knowledge and excluded the claimant from enjoyment.
predicates.statutory_period_of_hostile_possession_n: The claimant did not prove that the hostile possession continued for the legally required period.

issues.definition: A claim of adverse ownership against a coparcener fails where possession is referable to joint title and a known, exclusive hostile assertion maintained for the required period is not proven.

issues.legal_issue: A partition claim is not barred by limitation merely because a party alleges earlier possession or partition where the right to partition arose only after the estate became partible and the alleged earlier partition was not proved.
material_facts: The suit sought partition after the character of the land changed from impartible to partible following abolition and regrant.
The defendants alleged an earlier partition and continued possession as owners.
The appellate court disbelieved the alleged earlier partition, and the High Court held that the suit was brought after the change that gave rise to the right to partition.
issues.conclusion: The suit was not barred by limitation, and the High Court’s conclusion was upheld.
issues.legal_principle: The right to seek partition arose when abolition and regrant changed the land’s character from impartible to partible. The Court upheld the finding that the alleged prior partition had not been proved and that the suit was not time-barred; it cited no separate statutory provision or earlier case for this limitation ruling.

predicates.partition_claim_after_estate_became_part: A claimant brought a proceeding for partition after the estate had become partible.
predicates.right_to_partition_arose_on_change_to_pa: The claimant’s right to seek partition arose when the estate’s character changed from impartible to partible.
predicates.alleged_earlier_partition_not_proven: The party relying on an earlier partition did not establish that it had occurred.

issues.definition: A partition claim is not barred where the right arose when the estate became partible and the alleged earlier partition is unproven.

issues.legal_issue: The Supreme Court will not disturb a refusal to amend a pleading where the application was rejected for laches and the circumstances do not warrant appellate interference.
material_facts: The defendants applied in the High Court to amend their written statement to include additional land in the claim for repartition.
The High Court disallowed the application on the ground of laches.
The Supreme Court found no reason to interfere with that decision at that stage.
issues.conclusion: The refusal to permit the amendment was left undisturbed.
issues.legal_principle: Order 6 Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure was invoked for the amendment application. The Court declined appellate interference with the High Court’s laches-based refusal in the circumstances and at that stage of the case.

predicates.appeal_challenging_refusal_to_amend_plea: A party appealed against a court’s refusal to allow an amendment to its pleading.
predicates.amendment_application_rejected_for_lache: The court rejected the amendment application because it had been made with undue delay.
predicates.circumstances_do_not_warrant_interferenc: The appellate court found no sufficient reason in the case circumstances to disturb the refusal.

issues.definition: A laches-based refusal to amend a pleading remains undisturbed when the circumstances do not warrant appellate interference.

issues.legal_issue: A remand to determine whether property alienations were made for legal necessity may be upheld when that question remains for reconsideration.
material_facts: The appellate court remitted the matter for reconsideration of whether the alienations were made for legal necessity.
The High Court upheld that remand.
The Supreme Court upheld the judgments subject to the matters it separately decided.
issues.conclusion: The remand for reconsideration of legal necessity was upheld.
issues.legal_principle: The judgment records that the remand on legal necessity was upheld, but cites no separate statutory provision or earlier case as the basis for that ruling.

predicates.appeal_in_partition_dispute: A party appealed in a dispute concerning partition of family property.
predicates.validity_of_alienations_for_legal_necess: Whether the alienations were justified by legal necessity remained to be determined.
predicates.lower_court_remitted_that_issue_for_reco: A lower court remitted the question of legal necessity for further consideration.

issues.definition: When the necessity supporting property alienations remains unresolved and a lower court remits that question, the remand is upheld.
